title: Good to Great
author: Jim Collins
thesisParagraph: Greatness is not a personality trick, a sudden turnaround speech, or a lucky product break. It is the result of disciplined people facing reality, choosing a narrow concept they can truly serve, acting inside that concept with unusual consistency, using technology only when it accelerates momentum, and pushing long enough that outsiders mistake accumulated force for a breakthrough.

coreIdeas.name: good blocks great
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Comfortable adequacy can be more dangerous than obvious failure because it removes the pressure to change.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Notice where acceptable results are protecting a weaker standard from scrutiny.

coreIdeas.name: humble will
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The strongest leaders combine institutional modesty with a hard, almost stubborn demand for results.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Separate personal credit from professional responsibility.

coreIdeas.name: people before direction
coreIdeas.oneSentence: A strong direction is fragile if the wrong people are carrying it.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Resolve who belongs in the work before overcommitting to what the work must become.

coreIdeas.name: facts plus faith
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The durable stance is to face the worst true facts without letting those facts become surrender.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Hold reality and resolve in the same hand.

coreIdeas.name: disciplined concept
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Strategy tightens when capability, economic engine, and genuine passion meet in one lived concept.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Say no to attractive work that does not fit the three circles.

coreIdeas.name: disciplined freedom
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Great organizations give disciplined people room to move inside a clear framework instead of replacing judgment with bureaucracy.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Set the boundary sharply enough that people can act without constant permission.

coreIdeas.name: technology accelerates
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Tools matter when they amplify a concept already understood, not when they substitute for one.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Ask whether a technology speeds the flywheel or merely creates visible motion.

coreIdeas.name: flywheel discipline
coreIdeas.oneSentence: Breakthrough usually looks sudden only to people who missed the long sequence of aligned pushes.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Protect compounding work from reactive resets.

coreIdeas.name: durable greatness
coreIdeas.oneSentence: The leap matters only if its disciplines become strong enough to survive success.
coreIdeas.mentalMove: Turn achievement into institutional practice before it becomes complacency.

targetReader: Managers, founders, operators, board members, and ambitious individual contributors who have seen decent performance become a trap and need a stricter way to judge people, strategy, discipline, tools, and momentum.

signatureMoves: builds claims through paired-company contrast and disciplined comparison
uses sticky labels such as flywheel, hedgehog, clock building, and BHAGs
ties leadership claims to durable organizational habits instead of charisma
asks what keeps working after the founder leaves the room
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not turn the companies into hero-founder mythology.
Do not use a Collins label without the comparative test behind it.

voiceSpecimens: The flywheel moves because discipline compounds before applause arrives.
Greatness is less dramatic than the refusal to drift.
voiceAntiSpecimens: This chapter teaches leaders how to optimize excellence through transformational strategic alignment.
Jim Collins argues that organizations should leverage disciplined innovation to maximize long-term impact.
In today's fast-paced world, success is all about focus, passion, and being your best self.
Greatness is a journey, so take a moment to reflect on where you can improve.
The key takeaway is that good organizations need to think outside the box and embrace change.
teachingArc: The sequence moves from dissatisfaction with good results into the human foundations of greatness, then into truth-telling, strategic clarity, disciplined action, tool selection, compounding momentum, and finally durability. Each chapter narrows the reader's tolerance for theatrical fixes and trains a stronger habit: look at evidence, choose people and concepts with rigor, act within the concept, and protect momentum long enough for results to compound.
forbiddenMoves: Do not turn the book into generic excellence advice or a motivational call to work harder.
Do not make the company research sound like a formula that guarantees greatness in every context.
Do not treat humility as softness, discipline as control, or technology as either villain or savior.
Do not import detailed Built to Last frameworks into the closing chapter.
Do not praise greatness without naming the discipline that produced it.
Do not flatten researched contrasts into inspirational business slogans.
